claims.text: The initial system is an elemental Cr coating on a zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding substrate without an interfacial barrier.
A nanoscale deposited Al2O3 layer should be placed at the interface between the Cr coating and the zirconium-alloy substrate.
The Al2O3 interlayer will act as an effective barrier to elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion with the Al2O3 interlayer will preserve coating integrity in subcritical water.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion with the Al2O3 interlayer will preserve coating integrity during high-temperature steam exposure.
The relevant normal-operation envelope is approximately 300–400 °C in subcritical water over long exposure times.
The relevant accident envelope is approximately 900–1000 °C in steam for periods ranging from minutes to about two hours.
A continuous and adherent Al2O3 interlayer physically separates Cr from Zr and minimizes atomic interdiffusion.
Al2O3 is sufficiently chemically inert and thermally stable under the specified conditions to function as the proposed interface barrier.
The Al2O3 interlayer reduces the mobility of Cr and Zr atoms at elevated temperature.
Reduced Cr and Zr mobility limits interdiffusion and associated phase degradation.
Limiting interdiffusion and phase degradation preserves the protective properties of the Cr coating.
Compared with the unmodified Cr-coated baseline, the Al2O3-interlayered system will show significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Reduced interdiffusion will improve coating adhesion relative to the unmodified baseline.
Reduced interdiffusion will extend functional coating performance during prolonged subcritical-water exposure and transient high-temperature steam exposure.
Unmodified elemental Cr coatings on zirconium alloys suffer premature failure due to Cr–Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperature.
The long-term stability of the Al2O3 interlayer under repeated thermal cycling and mechanical stress is uncertain.
A controlled comparison at 350 °C for more than 1000 hours and at 900–1000 °C in steam for 60–120 minutes can discriminate the modified system from the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
Cr–Zr interdiffusion can be quantified using cross-sectional TEM and EDS elemental profiles, alongside adhesion and oxidation-resistance measurements.
The hypothesis is falsified if the interlayer produces less than roughly a 20% reduction in Cr–Zr interdiffusion, compromises adhesion, or accelerates degradation under the specified conditions.
